title: Weighed Against a Feather
sub: Grades 5–8 · ELA · Reading the scribe Ani’s words

hero.credit: Facsimile by Charles K. Wilkinson, 1922 · The Met

objective: Students will meet the weighing of the heart as the exhibition tells it through the Papyrus of Ani, made for a scribe about 1250 BC. They will read his words closely, in E. A. Wallis Budge’s translation: an urgent address to his own heart, and a patterned list of wrongs he did not do and good he did. They will name the devices that give the words their force, notice the translator at work, and write in the same form.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Some of the oldest writing people still read was written to be spoken at the most serious moment of a life. Reading it closely shows how repetition and pattern carry weight, and what one ancient people counted as a good life.

items.text: explain the weighing of the heart as Ani’s papyrus shows it: the scales, the feather of Maat and who stands in the hall
items.question: explain what happens at the weighing of the heart?

items.text: identify repetition, parallel structure and direct address in Ani’s words, and explain their effect
items.question: find repetition, parallel structure and direct address, and say what each does?

items.text: explain what a translator’s choices tell a reader: an old word, a bracket, an ellipsis
items.question: explain what a translator’s choices tell you?

items.text: write a short text in Ani’s form, choosing its structure on purpose
items.question: write in Ani’s form, and explain your choices?

materials: Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed: Ani’s words, set large, and the hall
Highlighters or colored pencils; differentiated handouts, one per student
connection: **Virtual visit:** open *The Weighing of the Heart*. Unroll Ani’s papyrus, meet the hall, test the rule, sort Ani’s words onto his two scrolls, then guess what the scales will do.
**Poster 2**, *Gods and Goddesses*: Anubis, patron of embalmers, and the heart scarab, carved with a spell to stop the heart “betraying” its owner.

steps.title: A heart and a feather
script: Show the room’s hall of judgement without explanation. Ask: *“A heart in one pan, a feather in the other. What could these scales be deciding?”* Take three or four guesses. Then read the room’s opening: *“Long ago in Egypt lived a scribe called Ani. When he died, his story was painted on a papyrus roll. It shows his heart being weighed on a great pair of scales.”*

screen.alt: The Weighing of the Heart room: a great golden pair of scales above a dark hall, with Ani and Tutu, Anubis, Maat, Thoth and Ammit standing below
screen.caption: The Weighing of the Heart

steps.purpose: Look and guess before anyone explains: what could scales like these be deciding?
students: What is being weighed against what?
Who do you think is watching, and why?

steps.title: Who is in the hall
script: Ani was a scribe who lived about 1250 BC; his Book of the Dead is now in the British Museum. Read the rule: *“A heart was weighed against the feather of Maat, the goddess of truth. The gods hoped the heart would balance the feather exactly, so the beam of the scales stayed level.”* Introduce the hall from page 3. The Egyptians thought the heart held a person’s will, feelings and thoughts: that is why it is the heart that is weighed.

screen.caption: The hall of judgement in Ani’s papyrus

cells: Ani comes into the hall with his wife, Tutu, his head bowed low.
Jackal-headed, he looks after the scales and watches the pointer.
Ibis-headed god of writing, ready with pen and palette to write down the result.
Goddess of truth, shown as a feather, or as a seated goddess with a feather on her head.
She waits by the scales: the head of a crocodile, the front of a lion, the back of a hippopotamus.

steps.purpose: Set the scene: the rule of the scales, and who stands in the hall.
students: Which figure writes down the result?
What do the gods hope the scales will do?

steps.title: Ani speaks to his heart
script: As his heart goes on the scales, Ani speaks to it. Read his words aloud twice, the second time slowly. Ask who he is addressing (his own heart, as if it were a person: **apostrophe**), what he repeats (**repetition**: *“My heart of my mother!”*), and what he asks (two commands: *make no stand*, *utter no lie*). The ellipsis marks words left out of the quotation.

screen.text: My heart of my mother! My heart of my mother! My heart of my being! Make no stand against me when testifying … utter no lie against me before the Great God, the Lord of Amentt.
screen.cite: The Papyrus of Ani, translated by E. A. Wallis Budge

steps.purpose: Read Ani’s words to his heart aloud, twice, and notice what he repeats.
students: What does he say twice? Why?

steps.title: I have not … I have …
script: Then Ani’s list. The dead recited a long list of wrongs they had not done, the so-called **Negative Confession**, before forty-two judges. Students hear the **parallel structure** of *“I have not…”* and the one line that breaks it. The **brackets** are Budge’s words, added for sense; *raiment* is an old word for clothing.

screen.text:
I have not lied.
I have made no one to weep.
I have not stopped water [when it should flow].
I have not taken milk from the mouths of children.
I have given bread to the hungry, water to the thirsty, raiment to the naked, and a boat to him that needed one.
screen.cite: The Papyrus of Ani, translated by E. A. Wallis Budge

steps.purpose: Hear the pattern of Ani’s list, and spot the translator’s marks.
students: Who added the words in brackets?

steps.title: Read closely, then write
script: Students choose a handout. All three read the same words and end with writing of their own.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Sort Ani’s lines into *I have not…* and *I have…*, match old words to their meanings, circle the repetition in his words to his heart, and write one line of their own about a good choice.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Annotate Ani’s words to his heart, explain the effect of the list’s parallel structure and the line that breaks it, explain three translator’s choices, and write three lines in Ani’s form.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Analyze the address to the heart against what the Egyptians believed the heart held, argue why most of the list is negative, weigh Budge’s word choices, and write a list in Ani’s form for a character from a book they have read.

steps.purpose: Read Ani’s words closely and write in his form, at the right level of challenge.
students: All three read the same words and end with your own writing.

steps.title: The Field of Reeds
script: Tell the end: in Ani’s papyrus, the beam of the scales stays perfectly level. *“Thoth tells the gods that no wickedness has been found in Ani. Horus takes him by the hand and leads him to Osiris, and the gods give him a home in the fields of the afterlife, the Field of Reeds.”* Show Sennedjem’s wall: the Field of Reeds looked like a good Egyptian farm. A few students read a line they wrote, and say which of Ani’s lines still matters.

screen.work: Sennedjem and Iineferti in the Fields of Iaru
screen.artist: Charles K. Wilkinson, a copy (1922) of a painting in the tomb of Sennedjem, Deir el-Medina

img.credit: Facsimile by Charles K. Wilkinson, 1922 · The Met

screen.alt: A tomb painting inside a blue border of water: Sennedjem and his wife reap grain, pull flax and plough with oxen, above rows of palms, fruit trees and flowers

steps.purpose: Hear the end of Ani’s story, and ask which of his lines still speaks to us.
students: What does this picture of the afterlife look like?
Which of Ani’s lines would still matter today?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level student, who reads a line and explains its structure.
